title: Runtime KV cache memory leak: on-call retrospective + runbook draft
content:
Summary:

This is a working draft combining a short on-call retrospective and an operational runbook for the recent serving-runtime incidents where a slow memory leak in the per-request KV cache led to an out-of-memory (OOM) cascade under sustained high-concurrency traffic. The leaked cache entries caused long-tail GC, which increased per-request latency and triggered aggressive continuous-batching expansion. That batching behavior amplified KV cache pressure and produced a transient deadlock between request-processing goroutines and the cache eviction worker.

Goals of this doc:
- Capture timeline and symptoms observed by on-call engineers.
- Provide deterministic immediate mitigations for on-call.
- Propose a stable runbook for detection + automated mitigations.
- List long-term engineering work items and owners.

High-level impact:
- Several host GPUs dropped from the pool due to OOM (4 hosts over ~18 minutes).
- Client tail latency spikes for the hosted API (p95 -> 4x baseline).
- Automatic scaling/failover recovered capacity but caused cascading retries and increased overall cost.

Timeline (concise):
- 2024-11-04 02:12 UTC: First alert for host-memory utilization crossing 90% (alert: runtime-host-memory-high).
- 02:14 UTC: Multiple requests started exhibiting 5xx errors (OOM).
- 02:18 UTC: Autoscaler removed 2 nodes concurrently due to repeated agent failures.
- 02:23 UTC: Engineering on-call (Ava) began manual triage; observed unusual KV cache growth in metrics (kvcache.size_per_host).
- 02:28 UTC: Temporary mitigation applied: throttled new request admission (per-model qps cap) to reduce cache pressure.
- 02:35 UTC: A hotfix deployed: reduced default per-request KV cache retention window from 6h -> 30m for affected model family (deployed as emergency feature flag).
- 02:50 UTC: Memory usage decreased; no further OOMs.
- 03:30 UTC: Post-incident monitoring showed stable memory at ~60% host utilization.

Root-cause hypothesis (current):
1) A regression in cache key lifecycle: certain path through the request pipeline created synthetic keys with monotonic identifiers (session-scoped ephemeral keys) that were not being removed when request contexts finished.
2) The eviction worker for the KV cache uses an amortized LRU pass that relies on periodic GC signals; under high concurrency and continuous batching, GC signals were delayed and the eviction worker fell behind, allowing heap growth.
3) Continuous batching logic increased batch sizes when P95 latency spiked; larger batches caused more KV entries to be produced per scheduling window, amplifying the leak and pushing the eviction worker past its backpressure point, which introduced a lock inversion between the cache map mutex and the request-processing mutex, causing the transient deadlock.

Immediate on-call mitigations (play-by-play commands and checks):
- Diagnostic checks (first 5 minutes):
  - kubectl top nodes/pods to confirm memory hotspots.
  - curl internal metrics endpoint: /metrics?filter=kvcache to inspect kvcache.size_per_host and kvcache.eviction_lag_seconds.
  - Query logs: grep for "kvkey:ephemeral" pattern to measure leak rate.
- Emergency mitigation steps (order is important):
  1. Enable per-model admission caps: runbook script: /ops/bin/set-model-qps-cap --model model-name --cap 20 (applies to hosted tier only).
  2. Flip emergency flag to reduce KV retention window: curl -X POST "$CONFIG_SVC/api/flags/kv_retention?value=1800" (seconds).
  3. If hosts still failing, perform rolling restart of affected service on the host: kubectl rollout restart deployment/serving-runtime --namespace=hosted --field-selector=spec.nodeName=<node> (one node at a time).
  4. Temporarily scale down continuous-batcher parallelism: patch the configmap continuous-batcher.max-workers -> 4.
- Why this order: admission caps and retention window reduce new allocation pressure without requiring restarts. Only restart nodes if memory does not reduce in 10-15 minutes.

Detection rules to add (proposed alerts):
- kvcache.size_per_host > 70% of host-heap for 5m AND kvcache.eviction_lag_seconds > 30 -> high-priority alert (SRE-NEW-KV-LEAK).
- continuous-batcher.batch-size p95 increases by 2x in 10m concurrent with kvcache growth -> correlated alert.
- cache-eviction-worker blocked > 10s (metric exported via /debug/blocked) -> paging rule to on-call.

Runbook: automated mitigation sequence (for runbook implementation):
1. If detection rule fires, automatically set model admission cap to 50% of historical p95 qps for model family (automated via ops controller).
2. If memory hasn't decreased by 20% in 15m, reduce kv_retention flag for affected model family to 15m.
3. If still unhealthy after 30m, spawn automatic rolling restart of serving-runtime pods with a max unavailable = 1.
4. Escalate to eng-serving-runtime on-call (pager duty) with attached diagnostic bundle (logs + /metrics snapshot).

Post-incident engineering work (owners + suggested tickets):
- Fix the leak in key lifecycle: bug ticket SRV-2107 (owner: Devon Chen). Unit tests: simulate ephemeral key paths and ensure keys are removed on context finish.
- Improve eviction worker scheduling: SRV-2110 (owner: Priya Nair). Consider moving eviction to a dedicated goroutine with cooperative backpressure rather than relying on GC signals.
- Add lock-order changes to avoid inversion between cache map mutex and request-processing mutex: SRV-2112 (owner: Marcus Lee).
- Add observability: export per-key-type retention histogram and eviction latency: SRV-2114 (owner: Ava Martinez).

Mitigation validation checklist (post-fix rollout):
- Run synthetic load test that recreates concurrency and continuous-batching conditions (scripts located in infra-test/playbooks/kv-leak-smoke).
- Verify that kvcache.size_per_host saturates then stabilizes below 50% under 95th concurrency.
- Run 24h soak on dedicated staging with fault-injection (delayed GC signals, artificially delayed eviction worker) to assert behavior.

Operational notes and gotchas discovered during on-call:
- The per-request KV cache has two retention modes (session vs request); the leak was specific to session-mode when requests had early-cancel flows.
- Emergency retention flag is global-scoped by model-family; we need finer granularity to avoid unnecessary perf degradation for unaffected tenants.
- Rolling restarts are expensive during autoscaler activity; prefer admission caps first.

Open questions / tradeoffs to document:
- Tradeoff between eviction aggressiveness and cache hit ratio: reducing retention reduces hits for longer-running sessions. We need an offline evaluation to quantify tail-latency cost vs memory headroom.
- Should the eviction worker be preemptible or run as separate process per node? Operational complexity vs robustness.
- Do we expose per-tenant memory quotas to avoid noisy-neighbor leaks? (security/product alignment required).

Follow-ups and next steps (short timeline):
- 2024-11-18: complete SRV-2107 (leak fix) patch and land unit tests (owner: Devon).
- 2024-11-22: implement eviction worker refactor PR SRV-2110 (owner: Priya).
- 2024-11-25: add detection rules to PagerDuty and runbook automation (owner: Ava).
- 2024-12-02: schedule cross-team review with product on per-tenant memory quotas (owner: Marcus).

Appendix A — Useful diagnostic queries and commands:
- Check kvcache size metric (promql): sum by (node) (kvcache_total_bytes{model_family="<family>"}) / node_memory_bytes_total > 0.7
- Find top faulty keys in logs: rg "kvkey:ephemeral" -n --hidden | sed -n '1,200p'
- Force immediate eviction (debug): curl -X POST $SERVING_ADMIN/debug/kvcache/evict-now?scope=node

Appendix B — Links and artifacts:
- Incident Slack timeline: https://slack-redwood.slack.com/archives/C02ABCD34/p1709823456000000
- Incident Jira ticket: SRE-452
- Hotfix PR (emergency flag): https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1289

Notes: this doc is intentionally pragmatic and focused on operational runbook steps. Please add corrections inline or propose alternative mitigations if you were on-call and took a different path. After two edits we will promote to the canonical postmortem + runbook in Confluence and link the finalized tickets.

End of draft.
